summary: After the 2013 decision to make XML the canonical RFC format, plain-text renderings still matter for readability and archival. This informational document gives the requirements for the plain-text RFC format, building on the higher-level requirements in RFC 6949.

eli5.summary: Even with fancy formats, many readers like simple plain text. This lists what the plain text version of each RFC should look like.

subtitle: What the plain-text rendering of an RFC must look like now that XML is the canonical source.

tldr.problem: RFCs moved to XML as the canonical format, but plain text stays important to many readers and tools, so its rendering from XML needed written requirements.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets rules for plain-text output: UTF-8 with a Byte Order Mark, ASCII art only, pages of at most 58 lines, lines of at most 72 characters, and no running headers or footers.
tldr.outcome: It applies only to RFCs published after the format transition, and the details were expected to change as the publication tools were completed. It is updated by RFC 9920.

facts.label: Encoding
facts.value: UTF-8 with a Byte Order Mark

today: RFC 7994 is an Informational document and is updated by RFC 9920. It applies only to plain-text RFCs published after the format transition, and its details were expected to change as the toolsets were completed.

sections.title: Why Plain Text Still Matters
sections.content:
In 2013 the community decided to move from a plain-text, ASCII-only canonical format for RFCs to XML, with more human-readable formats rendered from it. The high-level requirements behind that change are in RFC 6949. Plain text remains one of the formats rendered from the XML, and RFC 7994 states the rendering requirements for it.

The rules do not apply to plain-text RFCs published before the transition. Three assumptions drive them: the old tools are complicated to change and often need manual work for page breaks, other formats such as PDF and HTML will offer markup and pretty printing, and the community has a large tool chain for plain-text files that should keep working where practical.

The document warns that the details are expected to change as the new toolsets are completed, and implementers must not expect those changes to be backwards-compatible.
sections.eli5: Many people still like the simple typed version of a document, and lots of their tools work with it. So the simple version stays, with clear rules for how it is made.

sections.title: Character Encoding and Figures
sections.content:
Plain-text RFC files use UTF-8 (RFC 3629), but non-ASCII characters are allowed only in a limited and controlled way. Many xml2rfc v3 elements carry an attribute for the ASCII equivalent of a non-ASCII string, and that equivalent is rendered in the text as described in RFC 7997. The file includes a Byte Order Mark (BOM) so that readers get in-band information about the encoding.

Artwork must be tagged with the XML <artwork> element, and ASCII art must be tagged type='ascii-art'. The plain-text format includes only ASCII art. If the canonical format has other artwork, the text output must point to the figure in the HTML version.

Authors may supply ASCII art for the text file and SVG for other outputs, but the RFC warns that two different diagrams for the same content can confuse readers. If the formats conflict, readers should check the XML and PDF files.
sections.eli5: The typed version can use a few special letters, but pictures are only allowed if they are drawn with keyboard characters. Anything fancier gets a note saying where to look.

sections.title: Page and Line Layout
sections.content:
One plain-text output is created, with basic pagination: a form feed at most every 58 lines, counting blank lines. The community is to get instructions or a script to strip pagination if they prefer.

  • Headers and footers: front matter on the first page and back matter on the last page keep the structure from RFC 7841. Running headers and footers are no longer added.
  • Table of contents: lists section numbers and titles but no page numbers.
  • Line width: each line is limited to 72 characters, including indentation, followed by the end-of-line sequence. The RFC Editor uses CR LF.
  • Spacing: single-spaced within a paragraph, one blank line between paragraphs.
  • Hyphenation: hyphenated words such as Internet-Draft should not be split across lines.
sections.eli5: Lines are kept short, paragraphs have a blank line between them, and the page numbers and repeating titles at the top and bottom are gone.

sections.title: Building Text from xml2rfc v3
sections.content:
The plain-text formatter uses the relevant tags from the xml2rfc v3 source file to build a document that follows the layout and structure of the full RFC Style Guide (RFC 7322), including the updates in its web portion.

The process of converting xml2rfc v2 into text is described as well understood (RFC 7749), and the authors plan to rely on that practice when converting v3 (RFC 7991). The document calls out only what changes from v2 or deserves special attention: character encoding, page layout, and how figures, artwork and pagination are handled.
sections.eli5: The text version is not typed by hand. A program reads the XML source and writes out the typed pages following the style guide.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The plain-text format requirements involve no significant security considerations. The RFC adds one caution about the larger format project: unintended changes to the text during the transformation from the base XML file could corrupt a standard, a practice, or a critical piece of information about a protocol.
sections.eli5: The only worry is that the program could accidentally change a word while turning the source into text, and a wrong word could change what a rule means.

items.title: Page
items.text: A form feed at most every 58 lines, blank lines included.

items.title: Line
items.text: At most 72 characters including indentation, then CR LF.

items.title: Encoding
items.text: UTF-8 with a Byte Order Mark.

items.title: Artwork
items.text: ASCII art only; other art gets a pointer to the HTML version.
